q: בת 82, עצמאית ב- BADL וללא חסר קוגניטיבי. סובלת מסוכרת בשנים האחרונות. ברקע ידוע על אי ספיקת כליות קלה. המטופלת מעוניינת לדעת אילו ערכים מומלצים לה לפי הקווים המנחים, שפורסמו לאחרונה (מאמר SDANDARTS OF MEDICAL CARE 2020).
o: גלוקוז בצום עד 150, איזון לחצי דם של 140/80, HBA1C של מתחת ל- 7.5
גלוקוז בצום עד 180, איזון לחצי דם של 150/90, HBA1C של מתחת ל- 8.5
גלוקוז בצום עד 100, איזון לחצי דם של 120/80, HBA1C של מתחת ל- 7
גלוקוז בצום עד 130, איזון לחצי דם של 140/90, HBA1C של מתחת ל- 7.5
explanation:
**Targets in older adults depend on function, cognition and comorbidity**, not age alone. Table 12.1 separates healthy, complex/intermediate and very complex/poor-health categories, so interpret each target combination within its row (ADA 2020, p. S155).

**A. Fasting glucose up to 150, BP 140/80, HbA1c below 7.5.** Correct, according to the official key. The source-versus-scoring distinction below is retained; acceptance does not mean this combination is copied from a single table row (p. S155).
**B. Fasting glucose up to 180, BP 150/90, HbA1c below 8.5.** Wrong, the more permissive combination belongs to very complex/poor health; BADL independence and preserved cognition do not describe that category (p. S155).
**C. Fasting glucose up to 100, BP 120/80, HbA1c below 7.** Wrong, the table does not make this intensive combination the default here. A lower A1c target requires individualization without recurrent/severe hypoglycemia or undue treatment burden (p. S155, footnote).
**D. Fasting glucose up to 130, BP 140/90, HbA1c below 7.5.** Wrong, according to the official key. These limits match the healthy row; this is the documented distinction between source and official scoring, not a change to the key (p. S155).

**Official answer:** fasting glucose up to 150, BP 140/80, HbA1c below 7.5 (IMA, final answer key, 2020, question 62).

In ADA 2020 Table 12.1, Healthy lists HbA1c below 7.5%, fasting glucose 90-130 mg/dL and BP below 140/90 mmHg. Complex/intermediate lists HbA1c below 8.0%, fasting glucose 90-150 and BP below 140/90. No row gives the entire official combination (p. S155).

Note: Learn the table and official acceptance separately; the accepted combination does not appear intact in one row.

Source: ADA. Older Adults: Standards of Medical Care in Diabetes-2020. Diabetes Care. 2020;43(Suppl 1):S152-S162, p. S155, Table 12.1. https://doi.org/10.2337/dc20-S012

q: בת 84, עצמאית בתפקודה וללא ירידה קוגניטיבית ידועה. ברקע סוכרת ויתר לחץ דם. מה צריך לכלול הטיפול בסוכרת על פי המאמר Older Adults: Standards of Medical Care in Diabetes 2020?
o: איזון סוכרת עם המוגלובין A1C מתחת ל- 7.5% והערכה קוגניטיבית אחת לשנה
איזון סוכרת עם המוגלובין A1C מתחת ל-7% ואיזון לחץ דם מתחת ל- 130/80
איזון סוכרת עם ערכי גלוקוז בצום 100-200 ומתן טיפול בסטטינים
איזון סוכרת עם ערכי גלוקוז בצום 70-100 ובדיקת גילוי מוקדם לכף רגל סוכרתית
explanation:
Official answer: A1C below 7.5% and annual cognitive assessment.

**Treatment targets depend on function and cognition**, not age alone. For the independent patient with preserved cognition, the 2020 framework supports A1C below 7.5% and periodic cognitive screening. Cognitive impairment matters because it complicates glucose monitoring and medication adjustment (ADA 2020, pp. S153–S155).

"for adults 65 years of age or older at the initial visit and annually as appropriate." (ADA 2020, p. S153, Recommendation 12.3.)

**A. A1C below 7.5% and annual cognitive assessment.** Correct, both components are supported: the target fits the relatively healthy group, and Recommendation 12.3 calls for screening at the initial visit and annually as appropriate (Table 12.1; p. S153).
**B. A1C below 7% and blood pressure below 130/80.** Wrong, these are tighter than the stated framework, whose blood-pressure goal is below 140/90. A lower individual glycemic goal can be considered if achieved without recurrent or severe hypoglycemia or undue burden, but is not required for every patient like this (Table 12.1, p. S155).
**C. Fasting glucose 100–200 and a statin.** Wrong, a statin may be appropriate, but the proposed fasting range does not match this group’s 90–130 mg/dL target (Table 12.1, p. S155).
**D. Fasting glucose 70–100 and diabetic-foot screening.** Wrong, complication screening matters, but the proposed fasting range is below the recommendation for this group. Avoid hypoglycemia rather than choosing a tight target solely because diabetes is present (pp. S153–S155).

Source-to-key explanation: In older adults with preserved function and cognition and few comorbid illnesses, Table 12.1 gives A1C below 7.5%. Recommendation 12.3 specifies cognitive screening from age 65 at the initial visit and annually as appropriate, supporting both components of the official answer.

Read from the paper: ADA 2020, Table 12.1; Neurocognitive Function, Recommendation 12.3. [Article](https://diabetesjournals.org/care/article/43/Supplement_1/S152/30489/12-Older-Adults-Standards-of-Medical-Care-in).

q: Which glucose-lowering drug class has cardiovascular and kidney benefits described by Hazzard in older adults, while requiring caution about genital infections and diabetic ketoacidosis?
o: Treatment with DPP-4 inhibitors.
Treatment with sulfonylurea drugs.
Treatment with SGLT2 inhibitors.
Treatment with thiazolidinedione drugs.
explanation:
**SGLT2 inhibitors** lower glucose by increasing its urinary excretion and have cardiovascular benefits and effects that slow chronic kidney disease progression in the studies described (p. 1580). The source links genital infection risk to glucosuria and states that volume effects may contribute to ketoacidosis risk in susceptible patients. "There is increased risk for genital yeast infection and urinary tract infection, likely due to the induced glucosuria." (p. 1580).

**A. Treatment with DPP-4 inhibitors.** Wrong, DPP-4 inhibitors increase and prolong the action of endogenous incretin hormones. That is a different mechanism from the urinary glucose excretion linked to the combination of benefits and cautions described for SGLT2 inhibitors (pp. 1579–1580).
**B. Treatment with sulfonylurea drugs.** Wrong, sulfonylureas enhance insulin secretion, and hypoglycemia is their main adverse effect. That source description does not match the urinary glucose-excretion mechanism with genital infections and ketoacidosis discussed here (pp. 1579–1580).
**C. Treatment with SGLT2 inhibitors.** Correct, this class matches the source’s combination: increased urinary glucose excretion, cardiovascular and kidney benefits, genital infection risk, and a potential contribution of volume effects to ketoacidosis risk (p. 1580).
**D. Treatment with thiazolidinedione drugs.** Wrong, thiazolidinediones enhance peripheral and hepatic insulin sensitivity. Their stated adverse effects include fluid retention and increased heart-failure risk, rather than the SGLT2 profile described in the question (p. 1580).

Source: Hazzard’s Geriatric Medicine and Gerontology, 8th ed., pp. 1579, 1580.

q: A 79-year-old woman with diabetes and declining vision is diagnosed with center-involved diabetic macular edema. Which treatment approach is consistent with Hazzard?
o: Defer treatment until proliferative diabetic retinopathy develops
Treat the macular edema with intravitreal anti-VEGF injections
Prefer laser therapy because it has replaced intravitreal injections
Observe the macular edema because visual deterioration is slow
explanation:
**Center-involved diabetic macular edema** can occur at any stage of diabetic retinopathy. Intravitreal anti-VEGF agents provide effective treatment and have largely replaced laser photocoagulation for this condition; edema sometimes causes rapid visual deterioration (p. 1573).
"Intravitreal anti-VEGF agents (bevacizumab, ranibizumab, and aflibercept) provide effective treatment for central-
involved diabetic macular edema and have largely replaced laser photocoagulation." (p. 1573).

**A. Defer treatment until proliferative diabetic retinopathy develops.** Wrong, macular edema can occur at any stage, so proliferative retinopathy is not a prerequisite for addressing this diagnosed edema (p. 1573).
**B. Treat the macular edema with intravitreal anti-VEGF injections.** Correct, intravitreal anti-VEGF treatment is specifically described as effective for center-involved diabetic macular edema (p. 1573).
**C. Prefer laser therapy because it has replaced intravitreal injections.** Wrong, the source says anti-VEGF injections have largely replaced laser for this condition, not the other way around (p. 1573).
**D. Observe the macular edema because visual deterioration is slow.** Wrong, the source warns that retinal edema is sometimes associated with rapid visual deterioration, so the proposed assumption is unsound (p. 1573).

Source: Hazzard, 8th edition, pp. 1573.

q: A 66-year-old man reports four months of progressive erectile dysfunction. He has no known medical history but has lost about 18 kg over six months and reports polyuria, polydipsia, fatigue, and mood changes. Which interpretation of the metabolic symptom cluster follows Hazzard's description of diabetes in older adults?
o: Polyuria, polydipsia, and weight loss are inconsistent with diabetes presenting in later life
Polyuria, polydipsia, and weight loss suggest hyperglycemia and warrant blood glucose assessment
Diabetes presenting in later life is usually recognized from this classical symptom cluster
A history of classical hyperglycemic symptoms is needed before considering newly detected diabetes
explanation:
**Marked hyperglycemia** can cause polyuria, polydipsia, and weight loss. Older adults can present with these symptoms, although the most common presentation is elevated glucose found on routine laboratory testing; atypical symptoms are also described (p. 1566).
"The classical clinical hallmarks of diabetes are symptoms associated with marked hyperglycemia, including polydipsia, polyuria, polyphagia, and weight loss." (p. 1566).
"The finding of an elevated glucose level on routine laboratory testing is the most common presentation for type 2 diabetes in an older person." (p. 1566).

**A. Polyuria, polydipsia, and weight loss are inconsistent with diabetes presenting in later life.** Wrong, older patients can present with the classical symptoms, even though such a presentation is relatively uncommon (p. 1566).
**B. Polyuria, polydipsia, and weight loss suggest hyperglycemia and warrant blood glucose assessment.** Correct, the symptom cluster matches the source's classical hyperglycemic features; checking glucose is an application of that description, not confirmation from symptoms alone (p. 1566).
**C. Diabetes presenting in later life is usually recognized from this classical symptom cluster.** Wrong, the source identifies routine laboratory detection, rather than the classical symptomatic presentation, as most common (p. 1566).
**D. A history of classical hyperglycemic symptoms is needed before considering newly detected diabetes.** Wrong, routine detection and atypical presentations show that classical symptoms are not a prerequisite to considering diabetes (p. 1566).

Source: Hazzard’s Geriatric Medicine and Gerontology, 8e, pp. 1566.

q: A 73-year-old woman with diabetes is taking metformin and is hospitalized with a major acute illness that may reduce tissue perfusion. Which drug-related concern justifies avoiding metformin in this situation?
o: Development of hypoglycemia through stimulation of insulin secretion.
Development of lactic acidosis in the setting of impaired perfusion.
Development of hyperglycemia through increased hepatic glucose production.
Development of weight gain through an acute increase in appetite.
explanation:
**Metformin** primarily suppresses hepatic glucose production and rarely causes hypoglycemia when used alone (p. 1576). Hazzard advises avoiding it during hospitalization for major illness that may reduce tissue perfusion because impaired perfusion can precipitate **lactic acidosis** (p. 1576).
"Metformin primarily suppresses hepatic glucose production and may also enhance peripheral sensitivity to insulin." (p. 1576).

**A. Development of hypoglycemia through stimulation of insulin secretion.** Wrong, Metformin rarely causes hypoglycemia when used alone; the source identifies lactic acidosis associated with reduced perfusion as the concern in this acute setting (p. 1576).
**B. Development of lactic acidosis in the setting of impaired perfusion.** Correct, the source explicitly links major acute illness, decreased tissue perfusion, and risk of lactic acidosis to the advice to avoid metformin (p. 1576).
**C. Development of hyperglycemia through increased hepatic glucose production.** Wrong, Metformin suppresses hepatic glucose production rather than increasing it, so this proposed drug effect does not explain the precaution (p. 1576).
**D. Development of weight gain through an acute increase in appetite.** Wrong, the source describes decreased appetite and modest weight loss in some patients, not acute appetite stimulation and weight gain as the reason for avoiding metformin in this setting (p. 1576).

Source: Hazzard, 8th edition, pp. 1576.

q: A 78-year-old woman with diabetes, depression, and mild Alzheimer dementia attends a geriatric assessment. Her daughter reports missed medications and two hypoglycemic episodes requiring emergency visits. She takes metformin 1000 mg twice daily, glipizide 10 mg twice daily, sertraline 100 mg daily, and donepezil 10 mg daily. HbA1c is 6.8%, and recorded glucose values range from 65 to 280. Which change removes the sulfonylurea implicated by the source's warning about hypoglycemia?
o: Add insulin glargine while continuing the current oral drugs.
Discontinue glipizide in view of the recurrent hypoglycemia.
Add sitagliptin while continuing the current oral drugs.
Reduce metformin while continuing the current glipizide dose.
explanation:
**Sulfonylureas** enhance insulin secretion, with hypoglycemia as their principal adverse effect (p. 1579). Although glipizide may be safer than glyburide in older patients, Hazzard states that “all of these drugs should be avoided if there is concern about hypoglycemia” (p. 1579). Recurrent episodes make that warning directly relevant; metformin alone rarely causes hypoglycemia (p. 1576).

**A. Add insulin glargine while continuing the current oral drugs.** Wrong, adding insulin leaves the sulfonylurea in place, while insulin itself also poses a significant risk of hypoglycemia (pp. 1576, 1579).
**B. Discontinue glipizide in view of the recurrent hypoglycemia.** Correct, stopping glipizide removes the sulfonylurea in a patient with recurrent hypoglycemia, applying the source's recommendation (p. 1579).
**C. Add sitagliptin while continuing the current oral drugs.** Wrong, adding another glucose-lowering drug does not remove the sulfonylurea that the source advises avoiding when hypoglycemia is a concern (p. 1579).
**D. Reduce metformin while continuing the current glipizide dose.** Wrong, reducing metformin leaves glipizide in place; the source identifies sulfonylureas as a significant hypoglycemia risk and describes hypoglycemia with metformin alone as rare (pp. 1576, 1579).

Source: Hazzard 8e, pp. 1576, 1579.

q: An 83-year-old woman with insulin-treated diabetes and declining kidney function has episodes of hypoglycemia. Which relationship between kidney function and insulin treatment explains the need to review her insulin dose?
o: Declining kidney function increases the elimination of insulin
Declining kidney function reduces the exposure to insulin
Declining kidney function shortens the action of insulin
Declining kidney function reduces the elimination of insulin
explanation:
**Renal insulin clearance** matters when kidney function declines. Hazzard states, "Insulin is partly cleared by the kidney," and notes that the dose often requires substantial reduction in renal insufficiency (p. 1584).

**A. Declining kidney function increases the elimination of insulin.** Wrong, the source describes difficulty eliminating insulin in renal insufficiency, rather than increased elimination (p. 1584).
**B. Declining kidney function reduces the exposure to insulin.** Wrong, inference from impaired elimination: reduced exposure does not explain the source's warning about hypoglycemia and the need to reduce insulin doses (p. 1584).
**C. Declining kidney function shortens the action of insulin.** Wrong, inference from impaired elimination: shortening of insulin action does not explain the source's warning about hypoglycemia and dose reduction (p. 1584).
**D. Declining kidney function reduces the elimination of insulin.** Correct, reduced elimination is the stated renal mechanism relevant to her insulin-associated hypoglycemia (p. 1584).

Source: Hazzard 8e, pp. 1584.

q: A 74-year-old woman with diabetes and HbA1c 7.2% reports dizziness and near-falls. She takes metformin 1000 mg twice daily, glipizide 5 mg daily, and lisinopril 10 mg daily, and recently began tramadol 50 mg three times daily for osteoarthritis pain. Pre-lunch glucose values are 68–75 mg/dL. When reviewing glipizide because of concern about hypoglycemia, which statement follows Hazzard?
o: Withdraw glipizide because sulfonylureas should be avoided when hypoglycemia is a concern
Continue glipizide because pancreatic insulin release is not part of its mechanism of action
Continue glipizide because hypoglycemia is not an adverse effect of its drug class
Substitute glyburide because its longer half-life lowers hypoglycemia risk in older people
explanation:
**Sulfonylureas** enhance pancreatic insulin secretion, and hypoglycemia is their main adverse effect. Although glipizide may be safer than glyburide in older people, the chapter advises avoiding the class when there is concern about hypoglycemia (p. 1579).
"Their primary mechanism of action is to enhance insulin secretion by the β-cells of the endocrine pancreas." (p. 1579).
"Sulfonylurea drugs have established a long record of safety, with hypoglycemia being the main adverse effect." (p. 1579).

**A. Withdraw glipizide because sulfonylureas should be avoided when hypoglycemia is a concern.** Correct, this applies the source's class-level advice to the glucose concern in the stem without attributing every symptom to one drug (p. 1579).
**B. Continue glipizide because pancreatic insulin release is not part of its mechanism of action.** Wrong, enhancing insulin secretion by pancreatic beta cells is the stated primary mechanism of sulfonylureas (p. 1579).
**C. Continue glipizide because hypoglycemia is not an adverse effect of its drug class.** Wrong, hypoglycemia is explicitly the main adverse effect of this class (p. 1579).
**D. Substitute glyburide because its longer half-life lowers hypoglycemia risk in older people.** Wrong, glyburide's long half-life is associated with higher, not lower, hypoglycemia risk in older patients (p. 1579).

Source: Hazzard’s Geriatric Medicine and Gerontology, 8e, pp. 1579.

q: A woman taking metformin is hospitalized with a severe acute illness that reduces tissue perfusion. Which risk explains avoiding metformin in this setting?
o: Lactic acidosis in the setting of reduced tissue perfusion
Excess insulin in the setting of pancreatic stimulation
Metabolic alkalosis in the setting of increased acid loss
Fluid overload in the setting of increased sodium retention
explanation:
**Lactic acidosis** is the complication underlying this precaution. Although rare with metformin, it is the stated concern during major acute illness with impaired tissue perfusion (p. 1576). The source identifies "decreased tissue perfusion as a precipitating factor for lactic acidosis." (p. 1576).

**A. Lactic acidosis in the setting of reduced tissue perfusion.** Correct, the source explicitly connects reduced perfusion during major illness with the lactic-acidosis risk underlying avoidance of metformin (p. 1576).
**B. Excess insulin in the setting of pancreatic stimulation.** Wrong, the precaution asked about concerns lactic acidosis with impaired perfusion, rather than excess insulin from pancreatic stimulation (p. 1576).
**C. Metabolic alkalosis in the setting of increased acid loss.** Wrong, the source identifies lactic acidosis, rather than alkalosis from acid loss, as the complication relevant to this setting (p. 1576).
**D. Fluid overload in the setting of increased sodium retention.** Wrong, sodium retention is not the risk on which this stated metformin precaution is based; the source specifies lactic acidosis (p. 1576).

Source: Hazzard, 8th edition, pp. 1576.

q: During medication review for an older adult with recurrent hypoglycemia, which glucose-lowering drug class does Hazzard advise avoiding when hypoglycemia is a concern?
o: Treatment with DPP-4 inhibitors.
Treatment with sulfonylurea drugs.
Treatment with SGLT2 inhibitors.
Treatment with GLP-1 agonists.
explanation:
**Sulfonylureas** enhance insulin secretion and have hypoglycemia as their main adverse effect (p. 1579). Hazzard states that glipizide may be safer in older patients than other drugs in the class but still advises avoiding the class when hypoglycemia is a concern. "Glipizide may be safer to use in older patients, but all of these drugs should be avoided if there is concern about hypoglycemia." (p. 1579).

**A. Treatment with DPP-4 inhibitors.** Wrong, DPP-4 inhibitors rarely cause hypoglycemia when used alone: their incretin-mediated effect on insulin secretion decreases as glucose falls. That description does not match the class-specific avoidance statement asked about here (p. 1579).
**B. Treatment with sulfonylurea drugs.** Correct, the source’s avoidance statement applies to sulfonylureas, including glipizide, when hypoglycemia is a concern. Their insulin-secretory action and hypoglycemia adverse effect directly address the problem in the stem (p. 1579).
**C. Treatment with SGLT2 inhibitors.** Wrong, SGLT2 inhibitors are described as rarely causing hypoglycemia and lower glucose by increasing urinary glucose excretion. They are not the class targeted by the source’s sulfonylurea avoidance statement (p. 1580).
**D. Treatment with GLP-1 agonists.** Wrong, GLP-1 agonists enhance glucose-dependent insulin secretion and are described as rarely causing hypoglycemia. That is different from the sulfonylurea warning being tested (p. 1580).

Source: Hazzard’s Geriatric Medicine and Gerontology, 8th ed., pp. 1579, 1580.

q: A 76-year-old woman with diabetes and hypertension is brought by her daughter because she leaves the stove on and forgets medications. MMSE is 24/30 with memory and orientation deficits. HbA1c is 9.2%. She takes metformin 1000 mg twice daily, glyburide 10 mg twice daily, and lisinopril 20 mg daily. BP is 142/84 and Cockcroft–Gault creatinine clearance is 48 mL/min. Which paired approach best reflects Hazzard’s concerns about drug choice and treatment intensity?
o: Retain glyburide for its short half-life; consider less intensive glycemic targets
Avoid glyburide for its hypoglycemia risk; intensify treatment because of cognitive impairment
Avoid glyburide for its hypoglycemia risk; consider less intensive glycemic targets
Retain glyburide for its short half-life; intensify treatment because of cognitive impairment
explanation:
**Hypoglycemia risk and self-management capacity** must inform treatment planning (pp. 1568–1569, 1579). Hazzard states that glyburide is associated with higher hypoglycemia risk because of its long half-life and "is not recommended in this population" (p. 1579). Cognitive impairment can interfere with complex treatment tasks and may preclude an intensive program (pp. 1568–1569); this supports reassessing the target and regimen, not ignoring her hyperglycemia.

**A. Retain glyburide for its short half-life; consider less intensive glycemic targets.** Wrong, a less intensive target merits consideration, but glyburide has a long half-life and higher hypoglycemia risk in older people (pp. 1569, 1579).
**B. Avoid glyburide for its hypoglycemia risk; intensify treatment because of cognitive impairment.** Wrong, avoiding glyburide fits the drug warning, but cognitive impairment is a reason to reassess feasibility and safety rather than itself a reason to intensify treatment (pp. 1568–1569, 1579).
**C. Avoid glyburide for its hypoglycemia risk; consider less intensive glycemic targets.** Correct, both avoiding the flagged drug and reconsidering treatment intensity address concerns documented in the source (pp. 1568–1569, 1579).
**D. Retain glyburide for its short half-life; intensify treatment because of cognitive impairment.** Wrong, both rationales conflict with the source: glyburide has a long half-life, and cognitive impairment can make intensive treatment unsuitable (pp. 1569, 1579).

Source: Hazzard, 8th edition, pp. 1579, 1569, 1568.

q: An 84-year-old man with diabetes, stage 4 CKD (eGFR 22 mL/min/1.73 m²) and mild cognitive impairment attends the emergency department after a fall. His daughter reports three falls in the last month and increasing confusion. His medications are metformin 1000 mg twice daily, lisinopril 20 mg daily and zolpidem 10 mg nightly. Blood pressure is 108/65 seated and 92/58 standing; heart rate rises from 72 to 74. Creatinine is 2.8 and glucose is 68. Which action regarding metformin is supported by his renal function?
o: Discontinue metformin and reassess the glucose-lowering regimen in view of renal function.
Continue metformin at a reduced dosage with regular monitoring of renal function.
Divide the current daily metformin dosage into smaller doses administered more frequently.
Replace immediate-release metformin with an extended-release preparation at the same daily dosage.
explanation:
**Reduced renal clearance** matters when reviewing metformin, but **contraindication** is distinct from dose adjustment. Hazzard states: "Metformin is contraindicated in patients with eGFR below 30 mL/min/ 1.73 m2" (p. 1576). The same discussion notes the association of biguanides with life-threatening lactic acidosis in certain circumstances; the metformin table repeats the renal contraindication for the listed formulations (pp. 1576–1577).

**A. Discontinue metformin and reassess the glucose-lowering regimen in view of renal function.** Correct, the stated eGFR is below the source’s contraindication threshold, so continued metformin is inappropriate and its place in the regimen needs review (pp. 1576–1577).
**B. Continue metformin at a reduced dosage with regular monitoring of renal function.** Wrong, monitoring and dose adjustment do not override the explicit contraindication at this renal function; the source distinguishes that cutoff from general monitoring in CKD (p. 1576).
**C. Divide the current daily metformin dosage into smaller doses administered more frequently.** Wrong, dividing the daily dose still leaves the patient taking a drug contraindicated at his eGFR. The contraindication concerns renal function rather than the size of each administration (pp. 1576–1577).
**D. Replace immediate-release metformin with an extended-release preparation at the same daily dosage.** Wrong, Table 99-11 groups metformin and metformin ER under the same eGFR contraindication, so changing formulation does not address the renal restriction (p. 1577).

Source: Hazzard’s Geriatric Medicine and Gerontology, 8th ed., pp. 1576–1577.

q: A 76-year-old woman with diabetes and mild cognitive impairment has recurrent hypoglycemia while taking metformin, glipizide, and insulin according to glucose readings. The acute episode has been treated. Her eGFR is stable at 38 mL/min/1.73 m2, without acute illness or impaired perfusion. What should be the focus of medication adjustment to prevent recurrence?
o: Stop metformin while maintaining glipizide and insulin doses
Reduce glipizide and insulin according to glucose readings
Increase glipizide while maintaining the insulin regimen
Increase insulin doses while maintaining the glipizide dose
explanation:
**Insulin and sulfonylureas** identify patients at risk for hypoglycemia, whereas metformin rarely causes it when used alone. The source recommends regimens designed to minimize hypoglycemia and dose reduction when treatment is excessive; applied here, the change should focus on the hypoglycemia-associated drugs (pp. 315, 1574, 1576).
"outpatient diabetes regimens be designed specifically to minimize hypoglycemia." (p. 1574).
"individuals at risk for hypoglycemia (ie, being treated with insulin or a sulfonylurea drug)." (p. 1574).

**A. Stop metformin while maintaining glipizide and insulin doses.** Wrong, this leaves the insulin and sulfonylurea exposure unchanged. Metformin rarely causes hypoglycemia alone, and the supplied renal function is above the source's contraindication threshold, although renal monitoring remains appropriate (pp. 1574, 1576).
**B. Reduce glipizide and insulin according to glucose readings.** Correct, reducing the hypoglycemia-associated agents applies the source's dose-reduction principle; glucose readings guide assessment of the response (pp. 315, 1574).
**C. Increase glipizide while maintaining the insulin regimen.** Wrong, increasing sulfonylurea exposure intensifies a regimen already producing hypoglycemia, contrary to the stated prevention goal (pp. 315, 1574).
**D. Increase insulin doses while maintaining the glipizide dose.** Wrong, increasing insulin similarly intensifies treatment despite recurrent hypoglycemia rather than minimizing it (pp. 315, 1574).

Source: Hazzard 8e, pp. 1574, 1576, 315.

q: A 72-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes, hypertension, and recently diagnosed mild cognitive impairment (MoCA 22/30) receives home-based primary care. Her daughter found her unconscious twice in the past month, both times early in the morning before breakfast. She takes glimepiride 4 mg twice daily, metformin 1000 mg twice daily, and lisinopril 10 mg daily. Her latest HbA1c is 6.8%, creatinine clearance is 58 mL/min, and prebreakfast fingerstick glucose readings range from 68 to 95 mg/dL. Which approach to the sulfonylurea agrees with Hazzard when hypoglycemia is a concern?
o: Stop glimepiride and follow glucose to reassess treatment needs.
Continue glimepiride at a reduced dose to retain sulfonylurea treatment.
Replace glimepiride with glipizide to retain treatment from the same class.
Replace glimepiride with glyburide to retain treatment from the same class.
explanation:
**Sulfonylureas** increase insulin secretion, and hypoglycemia is their main adverse effect. Hazzard advises avoiding this class when there is concern about hypoglycemia, even though individual agents differ in risk; the low readings and episodes in this vignette make that concern relevant without proving the cause of the unconsciousness (p. 1579).
"Their primary mechanism of action is to enhance insulin secretion by the β-cells of the endocrine pancreas." (p. 1579).

**A. Stop glimepiride and follow glucose to reassess treatment needs.** Correct, discontinuation follows the source advice to avoid sulfonylureas when hypoglycemia is a concern; glucose follow-up allows reassessment after removing the drug (p. 1579; clinical application).
**B. Continue glimepiride at a reduced dose to retain sulfonylurea treatment.** Wrong, a reduced dose still retains a sulfonylurea, whereas the source advises avoiding the class when hypoglycemia is a concern (p. 1579).
**C. Replace glimepiride with glipizide to retain treatment from the same class.** Wrong, glipizide may be safer than other agents, but the same paragraph advises avoiding the whole class when hypoglycemia is a concern (p. 1579).
**D. Replace glimepiride with glyburide to retain treatment from the same class.** Wrong, glyburide is not recommended in older patients because its long half-life is associated with greater hypoglycemia risk (p. 1579).

Source: Hazzard 8e, pp. 1579.

q: A 77-year-old woman with diabetes, hypertension, and moderate Alzheimer dementia lives with her daughter, who has discovered medication errors. She takes metformin 1000 mg twice daily, glyburide 10 mg twice daily, lisinopril 20 mg daily, atorvastatin 40 mg nightly, donepezil 10 mg daily, and aspirin 81 mg daily. HbA1c is 7.2%, blood pressure is 145/85, and eGFR is 48. Which statement correctly identifies the source-described hypoglycemia concern in her oral diabetes regimen?
o: Metformin is the higher-risk drug because its main effect is to stimulate insulin secretion.
Glyburide is the higher-risk drug because its long half-life increases hypoglycemia risk in older patients.
Metformin and glyburide have similarly low hypoglycemia risk when used as single agents.
Glyburide is the lower-risk drug because its long half-life reduces hypoglycemia risk in older patients.
explanation:
**Glyburide** is not recommended in older patients because its long half-life is associated with increased hypoglycemia risk (p. 1579). In contrast, “Metformin rarely causes hypoglycemia when used alone” (p. 1576). The source therefore supports reviewing glyburide as the hypoglycemia concern; it does not establish a complete individualized replacement regimen from these data.

**A. Metformin is the higher-risk drug because its main effect is to stimulate insulin secretion.** Wrong, Metformin primarily suppresses hepatic glucose production and rarely causes hypoglycemia alone; enhanced insulin secretion is the mechanism described for sulfonylureas (pp. 1576, 1579).
**B. Glyburide is the higher-risk drug because its long half-life increases hypoglycemia risk in older patients.** Correct, this is the source's stated reason glyburide is not recommended in older patients and supports its review in this regimen (p. 1579).
**C. Metformin and glyburide have similarly low hypoglycemia risk when used as single agents.** Wrong, the source identifies hypoglycemia as the main adverse effect of sulfonylureas, while describing it as rare with metformin alone (pp. 1576, 1579).
**D. Glyburide is the lower-risk drug because its long half-life reduces hypoglycemia risk in older patients.** Wrong, the long half-life is associated with increased rather than reduced hypoglycemia risk, so it is a reason for concern rather than reassurance (p. 1579).

Source: Hazzard 8e, pp. 1576, 1579.

q: A 79-year-old woman with diabetes takes metformin. Her eGFR has fallen to 28 mL/min/1.73 m². Considering the renal appropriateness of metformin separately from treatment of congestion, which action follows Hazzard?
o: Stop metformin because the renal contraindication is present
Continue metformin because its hypoglycemia risk is low
Increase metformin because appetite and weight have declined
Switch to extended-release metformin and continue treatment
explanation:
**Metformin is contraindicated** when eGFR is below 30 mL/min/1.73 m². Its low hypoglycemia risk does not remove this renal restriction; Hazzard also discusses lactic acidosis risk and the need to account for renal clearance (p. 1576).
"Metformin is contraindicated in patients with eGFR below 30 mL/min/ 1.73 m2." (p. 1576).

**A. Stop metformin because the renal contraindication is present.** Correct, the stated eGFR is below the contraindication threshold (p. 1576).
**B. Continue metformin because its hypoglycemia risk is low.** Wrong, low hypoglycemia risk does not override the separate contraindication in reduced renal function (p. 1576).
**C. Increase metformin because appetite and weight have declined.** Wrong, dose escalation does not address the renal contraindication; the source also treats appetite and weight loss as potential adverse effects (p. 1576).
**D. Switch to extended-release metformin and continue treatment.** Wrong, the contraindication applies to metformin; changing its release formulation does not meet the renal requirement (inference, p. 1576).

Source: Hazzard 8e, pp. 1576.

q: An 81-year-old man with hypertension, type 2 diabetes, and stage 3a chronic kidney disease (eGFR 48 mL/min/1.73 m²) is assessed before elective hip replacement. He takes metformin 1000 mg twice daily, lisinopril 20 mg daily, and aspirin 81 mg. Preoperative tests show creatinine 1.8 mg/dL, potassium 4.2, and glucose 156. He lives alone and manages his medications, but his daughter reports that he has recently been forgetting appointments. Which principle should guide the metformin safety review around surgery?
o: Continue metformin during major acute illness because reduced tissue perfusion limits the risk of lactic acidosis.
Review renal function and avoid metformin during major acute illness that could reduce tissue perfusion.
Increase metformin when kidney function declines because renal impairment accelerates clearance of the glucose-lowering drug.
Use gastrointestinal tolerance instead of renal function to assess metformin safety during the medication review.
explanation:
**Metformin safety** depends on renal function and the risk of tissue hypoperfusion (p. 1576). Hazzard supports "Monitoring of renal function and perhaps dose adjustment of metformin to account for reduced renal clearance" in older adults with CKD (p. 1576). It also advises avoidance during major acute illness that could decrease tissue perfusion and precipitate lactic acidosis (p. 1576).

**A. Continue metformin during major acute illness because reduced tissue perfusion limits the risk of lactic acidosis.** Wrong, decreased tissue perfusion is identified as a precipitating factor for lactic acidosis, so it supports avoiding metformin during the specified acute illness rather than continuing it on this rationale (p. 1576).
**B. Review renal function and avoid metformin during major acute illness that could reduce tissue perfusion.** Correct, this combines the source's renal-function review with avoidance during major acute illness that could reduce tissue perfusion (p. 1576).
**C. Increase metformin when kidney function declines because renal impairment accelerates clearance of the glucose-lowering drug.** Wrong, the source describes reduced renal clearance in CKD and consideration of dose adjustment; it does not support increasing the dose because clearance is accelerated (p. 1576).
**D. Use gastrointestinal tolerance instead of renal function to assess metformin safety during the medication review.** Wrong, gastrointestinal symptoms are adverse effects to consider, but they do not replace the explicitly recommended assessment of renal function (p. 1576).

Source: Hazzard's Geriatric Medicine and Gerontology, 8th ed., pp. 1576.

q: A 78-year-old man with frailty (Clinical Frailty Scale 6), heart failure (ejection fraction 35%), and stage 4 chronic kidney disease (eGFR 22) attends follow-up. His wife reports that he falls asleep during meals and forgets medications. He takes metformin 1000 mg twice daily, lisinopril 20 mg daily, carvedilol 25 mg twice daily, and furosemide 40 mg daily. HbA1c is 7.2%, potassium 4.8, and creatinine 2.8. Which change addresses the metformin contraindication stated in Hazzard?
o: Stop metformin because renal impairment contraindicates its use.
Continue metformin and add a second glucose-lowering drug.
Increase metformin to improve glycemic control further.
Continue metformin and replace the antihypertensive agent.
explanation:
**Metformin and renal impairment** require a specific safety decision (p. 1576). Hazzard states: “Metformin is contraindicated in patients with eGFR below 30 mL/min/ 1.73 m2” (p. 1576). The source discusses the risk of lactic acidosis and renal clearance; this patient's eGFR is below the stated contraindication threshold.

**A. Stop metformin because renal impairment contraindicates its use.** Correct, stopping metformin addresses the explicit contraindication at his level of kidney function (p. 1576).
**B. Continue metformin and add a second glucose-lowering drug.** Wrong, adding another drug leaves metformin in place despite the renal contraindication (p. 1576).
**C. Increase metformin to improve glycemic control further.** Wrong, increasing a contraindicated drug does not address the renal safety problem identified in the source (p. 1576).
**D. Continue metformin and replace the antihypertensive agent.** Wrong, changing the antihypertensive agent leaves the contraindicated metformin treatment unchanged (p. 1576).

Source: Hazzard 8e, pp. 1576.

q: An older woman with prediabetes asks about preventing diabetes. According to Hazzard, what did the Diabetes Prevention Program show about lifestyle intervention in older adults?
o: It was less effective in older adults, and its benefit persisted during follow-up
It was more effective in older adults, and its benefit faded after treatment ended
It was more effective in older adults, and its benefit persisted during follow-up
It was less effective in older adults, and its benefit faded after treatment ended
explanation:
**Lifestyle intervention** was more effective in older than younger DPP participants. Older adults also had a reduced frequency of diabetes during long-term follow-up; the source associates this with maintenance of weight loss. (p. 1566)
"the lifestyle intervention program was more effective in people older than age 60 than in younger people" (p. 1566)
"The benefit of lifestyle intervention appears to be long term among older adults" (p. 1566)

**A. It was less effective in older adults, and its benefit persisted during follow-up.** Wrong, the intervention was more effective in older participants, so the proposed age comparison is incorrect. (p. 1566)
**B. It was more effective in older adults, and its benefit faded after treatment ended.** Wrong, the follow-up showed a sustained reduction in diabetes development rather than loss of benefit after treatment. (p. 1566)
**C. It was more effective in older adults, and its benefit persisted during follow-up.** Correct, both parts match the reported findings: greater effectiveness in older participants and a long-term reduction in diabetes development. (p. 1566)
**D. It was less effective in older adults, and its benefit faded after treatment ended.** Wrong, both parts conflict with the findings: the older group benefited more, and benefit persisted during follow-up. (p. 1566)

Source: Hazzard’s Geriatric Medicine and Gerontology, 8th ed., p. 1566.

q: A 78-year-old man has type 2 diabetes, hypertension, COPD, and stage 3 CKD (eGFR 45 mL/min). He takes metformin 1000 mg twice daily, glyburide 10 mg daily, lisinopril 40 mg daily, amlodipine 10 mg daily, tiotropium, and simvastatin 40 mg daily. He reports two falls on standing in the past month; HbA1c is 7.2%, and blood pressure falls from 128/76 sitting to 108/68 standing. Separate evaluation of the falls is planned. Which change specifically removes the long-acting sulfonylurea associated with increased hypoglycemia risk?
o: Replace glyburide with sitagliptin, using a dose appropriate for kidney function
Reduce metformin while retaining glyburide at the currently prescribed daily dose
Add fludrocortisone while retaining glyburide at the currently prescribed daily dose
Change antihypertensives while retaining glyburide at the currently prescribed daily dose
explanation:
**Glyburide** is not recommended in older patients because its long half-life increases hypoglycemia risk (p. 1579). DPP-4 inhibitors used alone "rarely cause hypoglycemia" (p. 1579), and sitagliptin requires renal dose adjustment (Table 99-11, p. 1577). The postural falls do not by themselves demonstrate hypoglycemia.

**A. Replace glyburide with sitagliptin, using a dose appropriate for kidney function.** Correct, this removes glyburide and uses a listed DPP-4 inhibitor with attention to its renal dose requirement (pp. 1577, 1579).
**B. Reduce metformin while retaining glyburide at the currently prescribed daily dose.** Wrong, reducing metformin retains the glyburide exposure specifically asked about (p. 1579).
**C. Add fludrocortisone while retaining glyburide at the currently prescribed daily dose.** Wrong, adding a treatment for hypotension does not remove the long-acting sulfonylurea (p. 1579).
**D. Change antihypertensives while retaining glyburide at the currently prescribed daily dose.** Wrong, changing blood-pressure treatment leaves the glyburide-related hypoglycemia risk unaddressed (p. 1579).

Source: Hazzard, 8th edition, pp. 1577, 1579.

q: An older woman in rehabilitation takes glipizide and has documented hypoglycemic episodes during poor oral intake. After the episodes are treated, which principle should guide continued use of the drug?
o: Avoid continued sulfonylurea use because hypoglycemia is a concern
Switch to glyburide to reduce the risk of further hypoglycemia
Continue glipizide because substantial risk is associated with glyburide
Increase the sulfonylurea dose when food intake decreases
explanation:
**Sulfonylureas stimulate insulin secretion**, and hypoglycemia is their main adverse effect. Glipizide may be safer than glyburide, but Hazzard advises avoiding this class when hypoglycemia is a concern (p. 1579).
"Glipizide may be safer to use in older patients, but all of these drugs should be avoided if there is concern about hypoglycemia." (p. 1579).

**A. Avoid continued sulfonylurea use because hypoglycemia is a concern.** Correct, documented hypoglycemia makes the source caution directly relevant (p. 1579).
**B. Switch to glyburide to reduce the risk of further hypoglycemia.** Wrong, glyburide has greater hypoglycemia risk in older adults because of its long half-life (p. 1579).
**C. Continue glipizide because substantial risk is associated with glyburide.** Wrong, a relative safety advantage does not remove the recommendation to avoid the class when hypoglycemia is a concern (p. 1579).
**D. Increase the sulfonylurea dose when food intake decreases.** Wrong, escalation is inconsistent with conservative dosing and avoidance when hypoglycemia is already a concern (p. 1579).

Source: Hazzard 8e, pp. 1579.

q: An 80-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes and mild dementia has weight loss and frequent falls. She takes metformin 1000 mg twice daily, glipizide 10 mg twice daily, atorvastatin 40 mg, and aspirin 81 mg. BMI fell from 23 to 19 over 8 months; HbA1c is 6.4% and LDL is 68. She forgets meals and struggles with cooking. Grip strength is 14 kg, and she rises slowly while holding furniture. Which adjustment addresses the hypoglycemia risk emphasized by Hazzard?
o: Stop metformin while maintaining glipizide and the current glycemic target
Stop glipizide and adopt a less stringent individualized glycemic target
Reduce atorvastatin while maintaining glipizide and the current glycemic target
Stop aspirin while maintaining glipizide and the current glycemic target
explanation:
**Hypoglycemia prevention** should guide diabetes regimens in older adults (p. 1574). Sulfonylureas carry hypoglycemia risk; Hazzard says they "should be avoided if there is concern about hypoglycemia" (p. 1579). Inference: a low HbA1c on glipizide with missed meals warrants reducing that exposure and revisiting the target; this does not establish that hypoglycemia caused her falls or that stopping it treats frailty (pp. 1574, 1579).

**A. Stop metformin while maintaining glipizide and the current glycemic target.** Wrong, this retains the sulfonylurea and current target despite the concern the question asks to address; the source identifies sulfonylurea-related hypoglycemia risk (pp. 1574, 1579).
**B. Stop glipizide and adopt a less stringent individualized glycemic target.** Correct, this addresses the implicated drug class and follows the principle of individualizing targets to minimize hypoglycemia (pp. 1574, 1579).
**C. Reduce atorvastatin while maintaining glipizide and the current glycemic target.** Wrong, changing atorvastatin retains both the sulfonylurea exposure and the glycemic target relevant to the stated hypoglycemia concern (pp. 1574, 1579).
**D. Stop aspirin while maintaining glipizide and the current glycemic target.** Wrong, changing aspirin retains both the sulfonylurea exposure and the glycemic target relevant to the stated hypoglycemia concern (pp. 1574, 1579).

Source: Hazzard 8e, pp. 1574, 1579.
label: Source: Hazzard 8e (marked) · p.1574

q: A 76-year-old man with type 2 diabetes and cognitive impairment needs treatment intensification. He forgets medications and meals and lives alone. Before selecting an insulin regimen for home use, which planning approach follows Hazzard?
o: Assess injection and glucose-monitoring ability together with caregiver support
Plan injections around his living arrangement without checking functional ability
Judge home feasibility from the dose schedule without assessing caregiver availability
Plan to begin glucose-monitoring education after insulin doses reach the target
explanation:
**Feasibility and hypoglycemia prevention** must be considered when planning home insulin treatment. Hazzard notes that injections may be infeasible because of "functional limitations or insufficient caregiver support" and emphasizes monitoring and patient education during initiation (pp. 1581–1582).

**A. Assess injection and glucose-monitoring ability together with caregiver support.** Correct, these are the practical abilities and supports that determine whether injections and glucose monitoring can be carried out in the home setting (pp. 1581–1582).
**B. Plan injections around his living arrangement without checking functional ability.** Wrong, living arrangements do not establish injection ability; the source explicitly identifies functional limitations as a potential barrier (p. 1581).
**C. Judge home feasibility from the dose schedule without assessing caregiver availability.** Wrong, a dose schedule does not establish caregiver availability, which the source identifies as a potential barrier to injections (p. 1581).
**D. Plan to begin glucose-monitoring education after insulin doses reach the target.** Wrong, the source calls for diabetes education with initiation and frequent early follow-up to avoid hypoglycemia, not delayed education after target doses are reached (pp. 1581–1582).

Source: Hazzard 8e, pp. 1581, 1582.

q: An older adult treated with insulin develops impaired vision and hand dexterity. Before selecting a self-monitoring device, what should be assessed according to Hazzard?
o: Ability to monitor glucose and manage hypoglycemia
Chronological age as the basis for device selection
HbA1c as evidence of independent device operation
Family preference as evidence of independent device operation
explanation:
**Self-monitoring ability** and recognition and self-treatment of hypoglycemia are essential parts of diabetes management. Visual and manual impairments can interfere with these tasks, making direct assessment relevant in an insulin-treated patient (p. 1574).
"Essential components of hyperglycemia management include patient self-monitoring of blood glucose (SMBG), CGM for selected patients, and recognition and self-treatment of hypoglycemia." (p. 1574).

**A. Ability to monitor glucose and manage hypoglycemia.** Correct, these are the tasks that the source identifies as especially important for people at risk of hypoglycemia, including insulin users (p. 1574).
**B. Chronological age as the basis for device selection.** Wrong, age alone does not assess the actual monitoring difficulties linked to the stated impairments (p. 1574; application).
**C. HbA1c as evidence of independent device operation.** Wrong, HbA1c is used to set and follow glycemic goals, whereas the question concerns ability to operate monitoring equipment and respond appropriately (p. 1574).
**D. Family preference as evidence of independent device operation.** Wrong, a family preference does not assess the patient's task performance, which the source identifies as important (p. 1574; application).

Source: Hazzard 8e, pp. 1574.

q: An older adult with stable type 2 diabetes is being considered for oral treatment. There is no acute illness, unstable heart failure, or renal contraindication. Which statement describes the principal glucose-lowering action of metformin in Hazzard?
o: It primarily promotes insulin release from pancreatic beta cells
It primarily delays absorption of glucose from intestinal contents
It primarily suppresses glucose production within the liver
It primarily increases excretion of glucose through the kidneys
explanation:
**Metformin** is described as primarily suppressing hepatic glucose production. The source states, "Metformin primarily suppresses hepatic glucose production and may also enhance peripheral sensitivity to insulin" (p. 1576). This is the mechanism relevant to the question; the patient's stated exclusions also avoid the contraindication contexts discussed on the same page.

**A. It primarily promotes insulin release from pancreatic beta cells.** Wrong, stimulating insulin release is not the principal metformin action identified in the source, which is suppression of hepatic glucose production (p. 1576).
**B. It primarily delays absorption of glucose from intestinal contents.** Wrong, delaying intestinal glucose absorption is not the principal metformin action stated on the checked page; the described main site is hepatic glucose production (p. 1576).
**C. It primarily suppresses glucose production within the liver.** Correct, this directly matches the source's description of metformin's primary glucose-lowering action (p. 1576).
**D. It primarily increases excretion of glucose through the kidneys.** Wrong, increasing renal glucose excretion is not the primary action assigned to metformin by the source; it identifies suppression of hepatic production (p. 1576).

Source: Hazzard, 8th edition, pp. 1576.

q: A 75-year-old woman with early Alzheimer disease (MMSE 24) and diabetes attends a routine review. She lives alone, drives short distances, and uses a pillbox filled weekly by her daughter. HbA1c is 9.2%, compared with 7.8% six months earlier. She takes metformin 1000 mg twice daily and glipizide 10 mg twice daily. Her daughter has found glucose tablets around the home and reports morning shakiness. During a review of possible hypoglycemia, which change removes a hypoglycemia-risk drug while individualizing her treatment goals?
o: Add sitagliptin to her existing glipizide regimen and retain the previous glycemic target.
Increase her glipizide dose and retain the previous target despite the cognitive difficulties.
Stop glipizide and individualize glycemic goals to cognition, hypoglycemia risk, and support.
Add bedtime insulin glargine to her existing regimen and retain the previous glycemic target.
explanation:
**Hypoglycemia risk and individualized goals** are both relevant to this review. Hazzard identifies insulin and sulfonylureas as the primary medication-related risks and recommends incorporating cognition, social support, and hypoglycemia history into goals; the stem’s symptoms prompt investigation but do not themselves confirm a hypoglycemic episode (pp. 1570, 1584; application to the stem). "The primary risk factor is iatrogenic: prescription of insulin or a sulfonylurea." (p. 1584).

**A. Add sitagliptin to her existing glipizide regimen and retain the previous glycemic target.** Wrong, adding another agent retains the sulfonylurea exposure and the prior goal; it does not accomplish the risk-drug removal and goal reassessment asked for (pp. 1570, 1584).
**B. Increase her glipizide dose and retain the previous target despite the cognitive difficulties.** Wrong, increasing the sulfonylurea retains the medication-related risk and does not individualize the target to the factors specified in the source (pp. 1570, 1584).
**C. Stop glipizide and individualize glycemic goals to cognition, hypoglycemia risk, and support.** Correct, this removes the sulfonylurea and reassesses goals using the factors Hazzard specifies; it is the change that meets the question’s two objectives, not a claim that stopping it completes diabetes care (pp. 1570, 1584).
**D. Add bedtime insulin glargine to her existing regimen and retain the previous glycemic target.** Wrong, insulin is itself a medication-related hypoglycemia risk, and this plan also retains glipizide and the old target; it does not meet the stated objectives (pp. 1570, 1584).

Source: Hazzard 8e, pp. 1584, 1570.

q: An 81-year-old woman with diabetes and stage 4 CKD (eGFR 22 mL/min/1.73 m²) is hospitalized after a fall. CT shows a thin acute subdural hematoma, and neurosurgery recommends observation. Her medications include metformin 500 mg twice daily, glipizide 5 mg daily, and lisinopril 10 mg daily. Glucose is 250–300 mg/dL on hospital day 2. The team selects basal insulin for glycemic control. Which plan follows the renal and insulin guidance in Hazzard?
o: Continue metformin and add basal glargine with glucose monitoring
Stop metformin and start low-dose basal glargine with glucose monitoring
Stop metformin and defer insulin treatment until kidney function recovers
Stop metformin and use glargine as the rapid-acting premeal insulin
explanation:
**Renal function changes drug selection**, while acute illness can make insulin useful for inpatient glycemic control (p. 1581). Hazzard states, "Metformin is contraindicated in patients with eGFR below 30 mL/min/ 1.73 m2" and permits insulin in renal insufficiency with dose modification and glucose monitoring (pp. 1576, 1581).

**A. Continue metformin and add basal glargine with glucose monitoring.** Wrong, at the stated eGFR, continuing metformin conflicts with the source's renal contraindication, even if insulin is added (p. 1576).
**B. Stop metformin and start low-dose basal glargine with glucose monitoring.** Correct, stopping contraindicated metformin and using monitored, appropriately dosed basal insulin follows the source's renal and insulin guidance (pp. 1576, 1581).
**C. Stop metformin and defer insulin treatment until kidney function recovers.** Wrong, renal insufficiency does not itself require deferring insulin; the source permits its use with dosage modification and monitoring (p. 1581).
**D. Stop metformin and use glargine as the rapid-acting premeal insulin.** Wrong, Glargine is described as basal insulin; the source instead identifies aspart, lispro and glulisine as rapid-acting premeal agents (p. 1581).

Source: Hazzard 8e, pp. 1576, 1581.

q: An 81-year-old man with diabetes fell during documented hypoglycemia. His oral glucose-lowering therapy is being reviewed to reduce further episodes. Which listed drug belongs to a class with a significant risk of hypoglycemia?
o: Oral metformin
Oral linagliptin
Oral glipizide
Oral sitagliptin
explanation:
**Sulfonylureas** are among the glucose-lowering classes with a significant hypoglycemia risk (p. 1576). Hazzard states that "only insulin and sulfonylureas pose a significant risk for hypoglycemia"; metformin and DPP-4 inhibitors have a different risk profile when used alone (pp. 1576–1579).

**A. Oral metformin.** Wrong, metformin rarely causes hypoglycemia when used alone, unlike sulfonylureas (p. 1576).
**B. Oral linagliptin.** Wrong, linagliptin is a DPP-4 inhibitor; these agents rarely cause hypoglycemia when used alone (pp. 1577, 1579).
**C. Oral glipizide.** Correct, glipizide is listed as a sulfonylurea, the oral class identified as posing significant risk (pp. 1576–1577).
**D. Oral sitagliptin.** Wrong, sitagliptin is a DPP-4 inhibitor; its class rarely causes hypoglycemia when used alone (pp. 1577, 1579).

Source: Hazzard 8e, pp. 1576, 1577, 1579.

q: A 78-year-old woman with diabetes and mild dementia lives alone. Her A1C is 9.2% on metformin; she forgets medications and meals. Her daughter requests insulin, but the patient does not want injections. Her MMSE is 28/30, although medication tasks require prompting. After reviewing her goals and arranging adherence support, an oral DPP-4 inhibitor is being discussed. Which description of this drug class matches Hazzard?
o: Oral treatment that augments insulin secretion even as glucose falls
Once-daily oral treatment that prolongs endogenous incretin action
Oral treatment that lowers glucose through direct insulin replacement
Once-daily oral treatment that is selected for a weight-loss effect
explanation:
**DPP-4 inhibitors** prolong endogenous incretin activity and are orally effective. Their insulin-secretory effect diminishes as glucose falls, explaining the low hypoglycemia risk when used alone (p. 1579). "These agents are used once daily and result in modest reductions of A1C." (p. 1579). This describes a treatment option, not proof that it is the best overall plan for this patient.

**A. Oral treatment that augments insulin secretion even as glucose falls.** Wrong, the source says the incretin effect on insulin secretion is reduced as glucose falls (p. 1579).
**B. Once-daily oral treatment that prolongs endogenous incretin action.** Correct, DPP-4 inhibition prolongs endogenous incretin action and permits once-daily oral administration (p. 1579).
**C. Oral treatment that lowers glucose through direct insulin replacement.** Wrong, the mechanism is enhancement of endogenous incretin action, not replacement with insulin (p. 1579).
**D. Once-daily oral treatment that is selected for a weight-loss effect.** Wrong, the source specifically states that these agents do not cause weight loss (p. 1579).

Source: Hazzard, 8th edition, pp. 1579.

q: An 81-year-old woman with diabetes receives insulin and a beta-blocker for cardiovascular disease. Which beta-blocker effect is relevant to hypoglycemia safety?
o: It may enhance the counterregulatory response to falling blood glucose
It may impair the counterregulatory response to falling blood glucose
It may strengthen adrenergic counterregulation during a fall in glucose
It may preserve adrenergic counterregulation during a fall in glucose
explanation:
**Counterregulation** helps raise blood glucose during hypoglycemia. Hazzard notes that beta-adrenergic blockers can interfere with this response and advises avoiding their combination with insulin or a sulfonylurea when alternatives are possible (p. 1584).
"β-adrenergic blocking drugs can potentially interfere with counterregulation of hypoglycemia." (p. 1584).
"Given the substantial benefit of β-adrenergic blockade to patients with CVD, combination with insulin or a sulfonylurea should be avoided and other glucose-lowering drugs used if possible." (p. 1584).

**A. It may enhance the counterregulatory response to falling blood glucose.** Wrong, the described effect is interference with the response, not enhancement (p. 1584).
**B. It may impair the counterregulatory response to falling blood glucose.** Correct, the source specifically identifies potential interference with counterregulation of hypoglycemia (p. 1584).
**C. It may strengthen adrenergic counterregulation during a fall in glucose.** Wrong, beta-adrenergic blockade can interfere with this response; strengthened adrenergic counterregulation does not match the stated effect (p. 1584).
**D. It may preserve adrenergic counterregulation during a fall in glucose.** Wrong, the source warns that beta blockade can interfere with counterregulation, so preservation is not the effect identified by the passage (p. 1584).

Source: Hazzard 8e, pp. 1584.

q: An older patient with diabetes and chronic kidney disease takes metformin and has an estimated glomerular filtration rate of 32 mL/min/1.73 m². Which monitoring principle is consistent with Hazzard?
o: Review renal function and dose in relation to reduced renal clearance
Increase the metformin dose to compensate for reduced clearance through the kidneys
Stop metformin and change to insulin on the basis of this value
Continue the dose and monitor glucose in place of assessing renal clearance
explanation:
**Metformin monitoring in chronic kidney disease** includes renal-function assessment and possible dose adjustment for reduced clearance (p. 1576). Hazzard states: "Metformin is contraindicated in patients with eGFR below 30 mL/min/ 1.73 m2" (p. 1576). The value in this stem is above that threshold, so it does not by itself meet the stated renal contraindication; it remains a reason to review renal function and dosing.

**A. Review renal function and dose in relation to reduced renal clearance.** Correct, this follows the source’s recommendation to monitor renal function and assess dose adjustment for reduced metformin clearance in older patients with chronic kidney disease (p. 1576).
**B. Increase the metformin dose to compensate for reduced clearance through the kidneys.** Wrong, inference from the renal-clearance principle: slower clearance is a reason to review exposure and dosing, not to increase the dose to compensate for reduced elimination (p. 1576).
**C. Stop metformin and change to insulin on the basis of this value.** Wrong, the stated renal contraindication is below 30, whereas this value is 32; the source does not make this value alone a reason to change to insulin (p. 1576).
**D. Continue the dose and monitor glucose in place of assessing renal clearance.** Wrong, glucose monitoring does not perform the renal-function monitoring specifically recommended for metformin dosing in chronic kidney disease (p. 1576).

Source: Hazzard’s Geriatric Medicine and Gerontology, 8th ed., pp. 1576.

q: An older adult taking metformin is hospitalized with severe diarrhea, dehydration, and acute deterioration in kidney function. How should metformin be managed during this acute illness according to Hazzard?
o: Continue metformin to take advantage of its effect on appetite
Withhold metformin because of the risk of lactic acidosis
Increase metformin to compensate for the reduction in tissue perfusion
Continue metformin on the basis of its low hypoglycemia risk
explanation:
**Metformin safety during acute illness** depends on more than its low risk of hypoglycemia. Hazzard advises avoiding it during hospitalization for major illness that could reduce tissue perfusion and precipitate lactic acidosis; renal clearance also matters (p. 1576).
"during acute hospitalization for any major illness that could result in decreased tissue perfusion as a precipitating factor for lactic acidosis." (p. 1576).

**A. Continue metformin to take advantage of its effect on appetite.** Wrong, the appetite effect does not justify continuing a drug that should be avoided during a major illness threatening tissue perfusion (p. 1576).
**B. Withhold metformin because of the risk of lactic acidosis.** Correct, the dehydration and acute renal deterioration in the stem make the source's acute-illness and reduced-clearance precautions relevant (p. 1576).
**C. Increase metformin to compensate for the reduction in tissue perfusion.** Wrong, reduced tissue perfusion is a reason to avoid metformin during major acute illness, not a reason to increase it (p. 1576).
**D. Continue metformin on the basis of its low hypoglycemia risk.** Wrong, rare hypoglycemia with metformin alone does not remove its separate lactic-acidosis risk in the stated illness (p. 1576).

Source: Hazzard, 8th edition, pp. 1576.

q: A 76-year-old man with diabetes taking metformin develops a severe acute illness with tissue hypoperfusion around the time of surgery. What is the main reason to avoid metformin in this situation?
o: Concern about frequent hypoglycemia during metformin monotherapy
Concern about lactic acidosis during an illness with hypoperfusion
Concern about increased hepatic glucose production during metformin treatment
Concern about reduced peripheral insulin sensitivity during metformin treatment
explanation:
**Lactic acidosis risk** is the reason to avoid metformin during a major acute illness that reduces tissue perfusion. Hazzard identifies decreased perfusion as a precipitating factor, while describing metformin as a drug that suppresses hepatic glucose production and may improve peripheral insulin sensitivity. (p. 1576)
"Metformin rarely causes hypoglycemia when used alone." (p. 1576)
"during acute hospitalization for any major illness that could result in decreased tissue perfusion as a precipitating factor for lactic acidosis." (p. 1576)

**A. Concern about frequent hypoglycemia during metformin monotherapy.** Wrong, Hazzard states that metformin rarely causes hypoglycemia when used alone; this is not the reason given for avoidance during hypoperfusion. (p. 1576)
**B. Concern about lactic acidosis during an illness with hypoperfusion.** Correct, the acute illness and reduced tissue perfusion match the setting in which Hazzard advises avoiding metformin because of lactic acidosis risk. (p. 1576)
**C. Concern about increased hepatic glucose production during metformin treatment.** Wrong, metformin primarily suppresses hepatic glucose production rather than increasing it. (p. 1576)
**D. Concern about reduced peripheral insulin sensitivity during metformin treatment.** Wrong, metformin may enhance peripheral insulin sensitivity; reduced sensitivity is not the stated reason for avoiding it here. (p. 1576)

Source: Hazzard’s Geriatric Medicine and Gerontology, 8th ed., p. 1576.

q: An 84-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes, stage 3a chronic kidney disease (eGFR 45), and mild cognitive impairment is brought to the emergency department after her daughter finds her confused. Glucose is 42 mg/dL, sodium is 138, and creatinine is 1.8. Her medications include glipizide 10 mg twice daily, metformin 1000 mg twice daily, and lisinopril 20 mg daily. She lives alone and frequently skips meals. After the acute episode has been treated, which medication approach addresses the hypoglycemia concern described by Hazzard?
o: Replace glipizide with glyburide and review her meal schedule
Replace glipizide with a DPP-4 inhibitor; review metformin dosing
Continue glipizide and replace metformin with a DPP-4 inhibitor
Continue glipizide and metformin and review her meal schedule
explanation:
**Sulfonylurea-associated hypoglycemia** is a reason to reconsider the drug class. Hazzard states that “all of these drugs should be avoided if there is concern about hypoglycemia” (p. 1579). DPP-4 inhibitors rarely cause hypoglycemia when used alone because their effect on insulin secretion diminishes as glucose falls; renal monitoring and possible metformin dose adjustment are also appropriate in chronic kidney disease (pp. 1576, 1579).

**A. Replace glipizide with glyburide and review her meal schedule.** Wrong, Glyburide remains a sulfonylurea and has a higher hypoglycemia risk in older patients; replacing glipizide with it does not follow the source's advice to avoid the class when hypoglycemia is a concern (p. 1579).
**B. Replace glipizide with a DPP-4 inhibitor; review metformin dosing.** Correct, this removes the implicated sulfonylurea, uses a class with low intrinsic hypoglycemia risk, and reviews metformin in light of reduced renal clearance (pp. 1576, 1579).
**C. Continue glipizide and replace metformin with a DPP-4 inhibitor.** Wrong, the sulfonylurea remains in the regimen; replacing metformin does not address the class that the source advises avoiding when hypoglycemia is a concern (pp. 1576, 1579).
**D. Continue glipizide and metformin and review her meal schedule.** Wrong, regular meals matter, but keeping the sulfonylurea does not follow the medication recommendation for a patient with a hypoglycemia concern (pp. 1576, 1579).

Source: Hazzard 8e, pp. 1576, 1579.

q: בן 78, מתגורר עם מטפל זר. ברקע סוכרת, יתר לחץ דם, מחלת לב איסכמית, מצב לאחר אירוע מוחי איסכמי עם חולשת צד ימין קלה, דמנציה מתקדמת, נזקק לעזרה בכל צרכי ה- ADL. אושפז במחלקה פנימית עקב אורוספסיס. בקבלתו לאשפוז HbA1C- 9.5%. הותחל טיפול ב- INSULIN. בני המשפחה הודרכו לגבי טיפול באינסולין. מה ההמלצות להמשך טיפול בסוכרת לפי המאמר Older Adults: Standards of Medical Care in Diabetes—2020?
o: סוכר בצום 90-130 מ"ג/ד"ל, יעד המוגלובין מסוכר מתחת ל- 7.5%
סוכר בצום 90-150 מ"ג/ד"ל, יעד המוגלובין מסוכר מתחת ל- 8.0%
סוכר בצום 100-180 מ"ג/ד"ל, יעד המוגלובין מסוכר מתחת ל- 8.5%
סוכר בצום 100-220 מ"ג/ד"ל, יעד המוגלובין מסוכרר מתחת ל- 9.5%
explanation:
**Advanced dementia and ADL dependence** place this patient in the poor-health group, where less stringent glucose targets reduce hypoglycemia risk. Table 99-6 supports fasting glucose of 100–180 mg/dL and HbA1c below 8.5%; for insulin users it also gives a lower HbA1c boundary of 8.0% (p. 1571).

**A. Fasting glucose 90–130 mg/dL and HbA1c below 7.5%.** Wrong, these tight targets do not account for advanced dementia, dependence and insulin-associated hypoglycemia risk in the poor-health group (p. 1571).
**B. Fasting glucose 90–150 mg/dL and HbA1c below 8.0%.** Wrong, this also remains too stringent for the category determined by dementia and dependence; with insulin, the table allows less stringent targets to limit hypoglycemia (p. 1571).
**C. Fasting glucose 100–180 mg/dL and HbA1c below 8.5%.** Correct, the combination fits the poor-health group and this patient’s limitations. With insulin, excessive lowering of HbA1c should also be avoided (p. 1571).
**D. Fasting glucose 100–220 mg/dL and HbA1c below 9.5%.** Wrong, targets above the stated range may permit glycosuria, dehydration and hyperglycemic crisis. Preventing hypoglycemia does not justify neglect of symptomatic hyperglycemia (p. 1571, footnote d).

Source: Hazzard, 8th edition, pp. 1571.
ref: Older Adults: Standards of Medical Care in Diabetes

q: בן 87, סובל מסוכרת שנים רבות. מזה שנתיים ללא טיפול תרופתי. ברקע – מחלת אלצהיימר, גר עם מטפל צמוד ומתנייד עם הליכון. המטפל מדווח שהמטופל מרבה לשתות ומטיל שתן בתכיפות גדולה. ירד במשקל 6 ק"ג בחודשים האחרונים. במעבדה המוגלובין A1C – 11%. על פי המאמר ADA Older Adults: Standards of Medical Care in Diabetes-2022 מה הטיפול המומלץ?
o: התחלת טיפול באינסולין ארוך טווח וטיטרציה עד לשיפור בתסמיני ההיפרגליקמיה
מעקב ערכי סוכר 3 פעמים ביום והתאמת טיפול באינסולין קצר טווח לפי טבלה
בגילו ובמצבו אין צורך להקפיד על איזון סוכרת
התחלת טיפול באנלוגים של GLP1 ומעכבי SGLT2
explanation:
In a patient with dementia and symptomatic hyperglycemia, the goal is **symptom relief while avoiding hypoglycemia**. Table 13.2 supports simplifying treatment, and the article presents **once-daily basal insulin** as a reasonable option in older patients, titrated to the individual goal (ADA Older Adults, 2022, Table 13.2 and Insulin Therapy).

**A. Start long-acting insulin and titrate until hyperglycemic symptoms improve.** Correct, this applies a simple regimen that can address symptoms with caregiver support, careful titration, and avoidance of hypoglycemia (Table 13.2; Insulin Therapy).
**B. Check glucose three times daily and adjust short-acting insulin using a sliding scale.** Wrong, repeated calculations and injections add complexity; the source recommends matching complexity to functional and cognitive ability and simplifying when needed (Table 13.2; Insulin Therapy).
**C. At his age and in his condition, diabetes control is unnecessary.** Wrong, avoiding tight control does not mean leaving symptomatic hyperglycemia untreated; the source explicitly identifies symptomatic hyperglycemia as something to avoid (Table 13.2).
**D. Start GLP-1 analogues and SGLT2 inhibitors.** Wrong, as the best choice here. The article cautions that GLP-1 receptor agonists may not be preferred with unexplained weight loss and notes volume depletion and worsening urinary incontinence with SGLT2 inhibitors in older patients, relevant to this patient's symptoms (Incretin-Based Therapies; SGLT2 Inhibitors).

Source: American Diabetes Association Professional Practice Committee. Older Adults: Standards of Medical Care in Diabetes—2022. Diabetes Care. 2022;45(Suppl 1):S195-S207, Table 13.2; Insulin Therapy; Incretin-Based Therapies; SGLT2 Inhibitors, doi:10.2337/dc22-S013.

q: בן 75, שמור קוגניטיבית ועצמאי בתפקודו, סובל מסוכרת מאז גיל 50. ברקע מחלת לב איסכמית עם סטנט ל-LAD לפני כעשור ואי-ספיקת כליות כרונית עם GFR של 52 מ"ל/דקה. המטופל שוקל 80 ק"ג (BMI 28). תרופות: INSULIN LANTUS 18 units+ APIDRA 6 units X3, RAMIPRIL, ATORVASTATIN, METFORMIN, ASPIRIN, EMPAGLYFLOZIN. במעבדה: פאנל שומנים בדם- LDL 68, HDL 34, Triglycerides 124 המוגלובין A1C -7.0 יחס אלבומין-קריאטינין 357 על פי המאמר ADA Older Adults: Standards of Medical Care in Diabetes-2022 איזה מבין השינויים התרופתיים הבאים יועיל למטופל?
o: הפסקת הטיפול בסטטינים בשל פינוי כלייתי לקוי ושינוי לטיפול ב- BEZAFIBRATE
הפסקת טיפול ב- METFORMIN מחשש לחמצת לקטית
הפסקת טיפול ב- EMPAGLYFLOZIN בגלל אי-ספיקת כליות
החלפת הטיפול ב- INSULIN APIDRA לטיפול ב- SITGALIPTIN (JANUVIA)
explanation:
The aim is **insulin-regimen simplification** while maintaining an individualized target, not declaring all good glycemic control in older age to be overtreatment. Figure 13.1 allows stopping mealtime insulin and adding a noninsulin agent when the mealtime dose is no more than 10 units; the doses in this stem fit that branch (ADA 2022, Figure 13.1).
"Discontinue prandial insulin and add noninsulin agent(s)" (Figure 13.1).

**A. Stop the statin because of impaired renal clearance and replace it with bezafibrate.** Wrong, the article recommends a statin unless contraindicated or not tolerated; the described renal impairment is not an automatic reason to replace it with a fibrate (Table 13.1; clinical application).
**B. Stop metformin because of lactic-acidosis risk.** Wrong, the article permits metformin at eGFR of at least 30 mL/min/1.73 m²; the stated value alone is not a contraindication, with continued attention to clinical status (Metformin).
**C. Stop empagliflozin because of renal impairment.** Wrong, the article describes cardiovascular benefits and slower CKD progression with SGLT2 inhibitors; the diagnosis given does not by itself justify automatic discontinuation (Sodium-Glucose Cotransporter 2 Inhibitors).
**D. Replace mealtime insulin Apidra with sitagliptin (Januvia).** Correct, replacing mealtime insulin with noninsulin treatment fits the simplification pathway, and DPP-4 inhibitors have low hypoglycemia risk. This does not claim zero risk or an automatic need for a reduced dose (Figure 13.1; Incretin-Based Therapies).

Official answer: ד remains the official answer. Source note: Hazzard qualifies SGLT2 use at eGFR 30-60 according to the product and notes limited data in this range (Hazzard 8e, p. 1580).
Source: American Diabetes Association Professional Practice Committee. 13. Older Adults: Standards of Medical Care in Diabetes-2022. Diabetes Care. 2022;45(Suppl 1):S195-S207, Figure 13.1, Table 13.1 and cited sections. doi:10.2337/dc22-S013; https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8935395/. Hazzard 8e, p. 1580, for the preserved source note.

q: What A1C level meets the diabetes criterion (Table 99-1)?
o: Only A1C ≥8.0 and <8.5%
explanation:
**A1C of 6.5% or higher** meets the diabetes criterion. The threshold is linked to the risk of diabetic complications, and the chapter does not lower or raise diagnostic thresholds simply because the patient is older. Confirmation is needed unless clear hyperglycemic symptoms establish the clinical context (pp1560–1561).
"diagnostic criteria for diabetes include a hemoglobin A1C level of 6.5% or higher." (p1561).
"the same glucose level cut points that predict complications appear to apply regardless of age." (p1561).

**A. Only A1C ≥8.0 and <8.5%.** Wrong, requiring this restricted high range would miss people whose A1C already meets the diabetes criterion at 6.5% or above; it would also wrongly exclude higher values (pp1560–1561).
**B. A1C <5.7%.** Wrong, this is the normal A1C category, so it does not itself meet the A1C criterion for diabetes (Table 99-1, p1560).
**C. A1C ≥6.5%.** Correct, this is the diagnostic A1C threshold; a qualifying result should be confirmed as appropriate rather than reclassified because of age (pp1560–1561).
**D. A1C 5.7–6.4%.** Wrong, this is the prediabetes category and falls below the A1C threshold for diabetes (Table 99-1, p1560).
